analysis.investment_thesis: Brigade is a Bengaluru-centric developer with improving operating momentum — revenue CAGR of 10.7% and EBITDA nearly tripling since 2016 — but real estate is an inherently capital-intensive, cyclical commodity business with no durable moat. At ROCE of 13.3% and Debt/EBITDA of ~3.3x, the returns on capital barely justify the capital risk, and the valuation at 24x trailing earnings is not cheap for this quality.
key_strengths: Multi-segment diversification (residential, commercial leasing, hospitality) smooths some cyclicality and adds recurring income from leasing
Consistent OCF generation — positive all 5 of the last 5 years — and a sharp equity infusion in FY25 meaningfully improved balance sheet headroom
Accelerating profitability: net profit grew from a loss of -96 Cr in FY21 to 680 Cr in FY25, demonstrating operational leverage
key_risks: Finance costs of 495 Cr in FY25 consume ~35% of EBITDA, creating significant earnings sensitivity to rate cycles and project execution delays
Debt/EBITDA of ~3.3x (net debt ~4,076 Cr vs EBITDA 1,630 Cr) exceeds my 2.5x comfort threshold for a cyclical business
Real estate development is a project-by-project business with no compounding moat — ROCE of 13.3% barely clears the cost of capital
red_flags: Net losses in FY21 and FY22 reveal severe earnings volatility — not the hallmark of a high-quality compounder
Free cash flow was only 66 Cr in FY24 vs net profit of 401 Cr — FCF/NI ratio of just 16%, suggesting earnings quality issues in that year
High promoter stake (41%) alongside large institutional ownership creates exit-event risk if sentiment turns
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Brigade has the look of a recovering developer riding the Bengaluru real estate boom, but inversion demands we ask: what happens when the cycle turns? The company lost money in FY21-22, its finance costs compound at the same pace as revenue (10.7% CAGR each), and FCF is volatile — swinging from 824 Cr in FY22 to just 66 Cr in FY24 before recovering to 358 Cr in FY25. ROCE of 13.3% means every rupee of capital earns just barely above a risk-free return once you adjust for cycle risk. The large equity raise in FY25 (equity jumped from 3,516 to 6,481 Cr) diluted shareholders and is a signal that capital needs are ongoing, not self-funding.

The leasing and hospitality segments offer some recurring revenue quality, but they are still a minority of earnings. At 24x P/E for a business with ROCE below 15%, cyclical earnings, and 3.3x Debt/EBITDA, I'm not getting compensated for the risks. A great business at a fair price is preferable to this — a fair-at-best business at a fair price.
